items.title: NYC is spending $70 million on 5 city-run grocery stores that will price essentials 30% below retail — and bodegas are fighting back
items.summary:
New York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026 that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow.

Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with nearly 1,000 supermarkets and more than 8 million inhabitants . But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices.

Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from independent grocers , supermarket trade associations and a coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses .

What explains this pushback?

As a food policy scholar , I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs.

The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has not operated independently of government . In fact, public policies and investments have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit,…
items.t: NYC is spending $70 million on 5 city-run grocery stores that will price essentials 30% below retail — and bodegas are fighting back

items.title: Meet ‘Captain Keel,’ the 37-year-old steering a Bitcoin miner into the AI data center gold rush
items.summary:
In late 2023, Bitcoin miner Ben Gagnon concluded that his employer, Bitfarms of Quebec, was in the wrong business. For Gagnon, Bitfarms’ greatest value lay not in the giant racks of GPUs that generated Bitcoin, but the immense power supplies it controlled. The then 34-year-old chief mining officer who’d launched his career crafting makeshift crypto-minting rigs in Hong Kong and Taipei, reckoned that Bitfarms could make much more money by exiting the field full stop, demolishing the “mines,” selling the chips that filled them, and re-channeling its plentiful flow of megawatts to power-craving industrial users at plants newly built on the Bitfarms sites.

The big revelation came in March of 2024, when Core Scientific and CoreWeave unveiled a stunning new deal. Bitcoin titan Core Scientific would refashion a mining facility in Austin, Texas, as an AI data center, and rent the power and buildings to the neocloud. That Bitcoin-to-AI play struck Gagnon as a model that Bitfarms could follow on a grand scale, from Quebec to Washington state. “It was the big aha moment,” recalls Gagnon. “Suddenly, we saw who the right customer was.” 

At the time, Bitfarms was mired in turmoil. In early 2024, the board was searching for its third leader in five years. The sitting chief agreed to depart when Bitfarms named a successor, but in May—believe it or not while still CEO—instead filed a $27 million suit for “wrongful termination and breach of contract,” plunging this Canadian exemplar of all-green, hydro-driven Bitcoin mining into legal warfare. Pounded by a sharp drop in the token’s…
items.t: Meet ‘Captain Keel,’ the 37-year-old steering a Bitcoin miner into the AI data center gold rush

items.title: Jensen Huang’s $145 billion question: What California divorce law says Lori Huang could get
items.summary:
Jensen Huang has lost his job, his board seat, and roughly $10 billion in paper wealth since admitting to an affair. If his 41-year marriage ends, California law could put a far larger share of his fortune in play.

Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s president, CEO, and director this week, days after confessing in a letter to Nvidia employees that he had been unfaithful to Lori Huang, his wife since 1985. The board named chief financial officer Colette Kress Nvidia’s interim CEO and made longtime director Harvey Jones its first board chair while it searches for a permanent successor.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang wrote.

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

The admission followed a New York Times report that U.S. intelligence agencies suspected Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, of gathering information for Beijing, and that she had a close relationship with Huang. China has denied involvement. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said this week that she left Singapore in February and was barred from returning after a police investigation, which it said “did not concern espionage.”

Two more relationships have since been reported. The New York Times reported on November 11 that Huang had been romantically involved with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reported directly to him, citing five people who had worked at the company. A day later, Reuters reported that Huang had an intimate relationship…
items.t: Jensen Huang’s $145 billion question: What California divorce law says Lori Huang could get

items.title: Tech companies are betting big on AI shopping, but Americans may already have bot fatigue as 72% don’t plan to use it for holiday gifts
items.summary:
Tech companies have spent the past year teaching AI how to shop. Google has introduced an AI-powered shopping cart , Meta’s Muse can search for products and prepare purchases for approval, and OpenAI’s new ChatGPT Wallet lets eligible users pay for purchases through an AI agent. Adobe expects traffic from AI tools to U.S. retail sites to jump 130% this holiday season.

Americans, it turns out, aren’t nearly as eager to hand over their gift lists. 

Nearly three-quarters of Americans, or 72%, say they don’t plan to use AI tools for holiday shopping this year, up from 49% in 2025, according to a new Bank of America survey . The 23-percentage-point jump suggests a gap between the industry’s ambitions for AI shopping and what consumers say they want from it. 

The reasons shoppers gave suggest that when it comes to gifts, efficiency isn’t the point. Among those who don’t plan to use the technology, 42% cited personal or ethical reasons, 37% said it takes away the personal aspect of gift giving, and 26% said they don’t trust AI recommendations. 

Lora Monfared, head of consumer credit card products at Bank of America , said shoppers may be growing more selective about when AI is worth using, especially as they keep a closer eye on holiday spending. 

“Some of last year’s curiosity about AI may also have worn off, and we could be seeing a bit of AI fatigue,” Monfared told Fortune . “Gift shopping is personal, and people want to feel good about what they’re giving.”

The survey found that 87% of Americans expect to spend the same amount or less on holiday shopping this year,…
items.t: Tech companies are betting big on AI shopping, but Americans may already have bot fatigue as 72% don’t plan to use it for holiday gifts

items.title: A $300 million logistics hub is betting Vietnam can move beyond the assembly line—if Washington lets it, and Hanoi can deliver
items.summary:
Yap Kwong Weng is a little frustrated with where U.S. tariffs on Vietnam are right now. 

“U.S. tariffs have changed three times this year,” the Vietnam SuperPort CEO tells Fortune . When the year began, tariffs on Vietnamese goods stood at 20%, as agreed by Washington and Hanoi as part of an interim trade framework in October 2025. Then, in February, the Supreme Court struck down the reciprocal tariffs U.S. President Donald Trump imposed in April 2025 as unlawful; Trump, in response, imposed a global 10% tariff on all imports.

Since July, most Vietnamese goods now carry a 12.5% import duty , following a U.S. Section 301 investigation into forced labor enforcement. Tariffs are likely to change again—either due to ongoing trade negotiations between the U.S. and Vietnam, or following further U.S. probes into industrial overcapacity and intellectual property protections.

“Companies now have stopped looking at stability,” Yap says. “Now they are planning for uncertainty.”

Yap is the CEO of Vietnam SuperPort, a joint venture between Singapore’s YCH Group, a family-owned logistics company, and T&T Group, a Vietnamese conglomerate. Based in Phu Tho province, north of Hanoi, the 83-hectare logistics hub sits on the corridors linking Vietnam’s electronics manufacturing belt to the Chinese border, where most of the components come from. The idea is that road, rail, air, and sea transit works as one service, so an exporter can tap one predictable route rather than four different modes. 

The SuperPort’s air cargo terminal is already operational, and Yap claims that monthly revenue…
items.t: A $300 million logistics hub is betting Vietnam can move beyond the assembly line—if Washington lets it, and Hanoi can deliver

items.title: The future of U.S. renewable energy rests on Nextpower—the backbone of the growing solar sector
items.summary:
Nextpower operates as the spine of the U.S. solar sector—and increasingly worldwide—by literally lifting the solar panels toward the sun. But maybe cofounder and CEO Dan Shugar would think of his company as the stem of the industry instead.

Nextpower specializes in solar trackers, the arrays and devices that operate in slow motion to keep solar panels oriented toward the sun, maximizing the solar panels’ energy production each day.

“The trackers do what sunflowers have been doing for millions of years,” Shugar told Fortune . “They basically follow the sun during the day, and they can produce almost 30% more energy. It depends on the location and the project design.”

While Nextpower controls 55% of the U.S. solar tracker market—and about 30% globally—the company has gone on a buying spree of late to enter the battery business and expand its solar portfolio to cover essentially everything except the actual solar cells.

The company is 13 years old but just changed its name last year from Nextracker to reflect its increasingly diversified business model.

“We moved from a pure-play tracker company, and we developed a platform strategy to do everything in solar except make the solar cells,” Shugar said. “And we’re doing everything in batteries except make the battery cells.”

Nextpower’s stock is up 12% this year to a market cap of $15 billion. Nextpower also was ranked 24 th this year in Fortune’s Fastest-Growing Companies list.

This month, Jefferies energy analyst Julien Dumoulin-Smith declared Nextpower as the firm’s “franchise pick” in the power and utilities sector…
items.t: The future of U.S. renewable energy rests on Nextpower—the backbone of the growing solar sector

Unilever had spotted in the 1960s that farming salmon, which until then was caught wild and remained a relative luxury, would create a mass market, lower costs and provide steady profits. By 1976, it had expanded into three Scottish sites producing 116 tonnes of fish each year.

items.title: FAA lifts ground stop as homeland security chief blames tech upgrades for ‘overwhelming’ antiquated systems and rules out cyberattack for now
items.summary:
Millions of U.S. travelers were suddenly thrown into limbo Friday afternoon after the FAA announced a nationwide ground stop at all U.S. airports.

Hours later, it was lifted, and federal officials used the incident to highlight the need for more funding to update aging systems.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy initially blamed a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.

In a White House press briefing later on Friday night, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin attributed the disruptions to technology upgrades, for “overwhelming” the antiquated equipment.

“It’s going to continue to fail,” he warned.

Despite recent hacking incidents of freezers in Europe and U.S. military bases, he said it “doesn’t appear” that a cyberattack was involved though he admitted that “there’s nothing certain right now.” Earlier, he ruled out a terrorist attack and said “This isn’t another 9/11.” 

Just days before the ground stop, the FAA announced it would deploy an AI tool to help air-traffic controllers

During the briefing, Duffy also suggested that the problem was related to old equipment being overloaded.

“Our fix gives us a pretty good indication that it was a legacy network problem that went down,” he said.

Duffy also called on Congress to provide emergency funding to fix the FAA’s aging systems, saying the Trump administration needs another $30 billion, then putting the price tag at $50 billion.

Still, the massive disruption comes as airlines in Europe suffered a wave of phony bomb threats this week. While they all appeared to hoaxes, at least…
items.t: Travel chaos worsens as communications problem causes ground stop at all U.S. airports while European airlines reel from wave of bomb threats

items.title: One Microsoft glitch stalled courts, government offices and police—exposing how fragile America’s systems really are
items.summary:
On Thursday, Nov. 12, a widespread Microsoft outage left millions around the world unable to send emails, open Outlook, or use workplace tools like Teams. At first it sounded like a corporate problem: unanswered emails, derailed meetings, employees unable to get work done. Some even welcomed the break. “Thank you Microsoft. Can you do this every Friday?” one X user joked .

But the damage reached far beyond the office. Police departments struggled to receive online crime reports, hospitals fell back on other ways to communicate, and some government services were suspended.

The disruption exposed how deeply governments and essential public services now depend on a single private company’s technology, and how something as ordinary as an email outage can interfere with the systems people rely on for public safety, health care, and justice.

Police, courts, and governments lost a key line of communication 

In California, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department reported disruptions to its email and other essential communication platforms. The Los Angeles Police Department and the county district attorney’s office also had email problems.

Law enforcement elsewhere was hit too. In Florida, St. Lucie County confirmed that its sheriff’s office and fire district were affected. Colorado’s Weld County Sheriff’s Office reported email problems and asked residents to call or text instead.

Across the Atlantic, British police forces including Dorset, Cumbria, South Wales, Wiltshire, and Dyfed-Powys had trouble receiving online crime reports, according to The Sun . Some forces said…
items.t: One Microsoft glitch stalled courts, government offices and police—exposing how fragile America’s systems really are

items.title: Air traffic control, phone systems and emails are all down following China’s AI espionage scandal — is there a common answer?
items.summary:
An old English proverb anchored in superstition from ancient Greek and Roman beliefs is that bad luck always comes in threes, but that does not mean bad luck was always random.

The United States has now experienced two debilitating, unprecedented blackouts across critical infrastructure in two days. The timing is almost too coincidental to be a coincidence – coming on the heels of the removal of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO amidst an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, widespread recriminations about chip exports to China, and demands for tighter export controls and more hawkish policies against China. 

Could China and other hostile foreign actors be targeting U.S. infrastructure? It’s too early to know for sure, but the country deserves far more transparent answers than we have received so far.

An extraordinary timeline, too coincidental to be a coincidence? 

At 3:54 p.m. ET on Friday , November 13, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded every departing flight in America, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” It was only the third nationwide ground stop ever ordered. The first came on Sept. 11, 2001; the second more than 20 years later, on Jan. 11, 2023.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy would say only that “a communication issue” had struck every one of the 22 centers that guide planes across the country, and that technicians were investigating. A subsequent press conference by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin did little to reassure anyone, with no answers about what happened and little reassurance that it would be…
items.t: Air traffic control, phone systems and emails are all down following China’s AI espionage scandal — is there a common answer?

items.title: The folly of just-in-time supply chains | Letters
items.summary:
Hannah Walker says systems designed to minimise expenditure in the name of efficiency can end up less capable of fulfilling their actual purpose

The widespread adoption of just-in-time supply chains illustrates it perfectly. By eliminating inventories and spare capacity, businesses reduced costs and improved efficiency, but frequently transferred those savings into risks that remained invisible until something went wrong. The disruption of global manufacturing during the pandemic exposed the consequences.

items.title: Fight the climate crisis or go for growth? There is a way Burnham can do both | Jonathan Freedland
items.summary:
The environmental and economic dilemmas he faces are formidable but, with a bold plan, he could set an example for leaders around the world

For politicians of the centre-left especially, it’s the great dilemma of the age. How do you do what everyone can see is essential to save the planet from boiling – even as your voters demand action to get the economy growing and to make life more affordable? Plenty of activists will tell you there’s no contradiction, that tackling the climate crisis makes economic as well as ecological sense and, in the long term, you know they’re right. But you don’t live in the long term. You’re running the government right now and facing several unavoidable, binary choices.

Andy Burnham is a prime example. This week, he addressed the Cop summit in Antalya, promising “a new era of British leadership” in the struggle against global heating. It’s important to him to talk that way: his political strategy relies on shrinking the appeal of the Green party, whose electoral success earlier this year helped remove his predecessor. But talk only takes you so far. Eventually the words have to be matched by action.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

items.t: Fight the climate crisis or go for growth? There is a way Burnham can do both | Jonathan Freedland

items.title: The Guardian view on venture capitalism: investor profits are no industrial strategy | Editorial
items.summary:
Higher returns for backers do not guarantee national prosperity. Public investment should develop domestic capabilities and meet urgent social needs

Britain keeps selling its most valuable companies. The Financial Times calculates that 300 went to foreign buyers, mostly American, over the past decade. What if innovation were scaled up to serve social needs here rather than US investors’ profits? That is the provocation issued by the thinktank Common Wealth in a paper titled We Aren’t the Champions, which takes aim at the UK’s venture capital (VC) industry.

The authors say that as long as the UK is subordinated to US cash, getting startups to a heavyweight size will be a sisyphean task. Britain’s tech pioneers are often sold before they become giants. DeepMind, founded in London in 2010, went to Google just four years later. Britain’s venture capitalists might argue that they are in it for themselves, not for building up British tech.

Continue reading...
items.t: The Guardian view on venture capitalism: investor profits are no industrial strategy | Editorial

items.title: Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go | Nils Pratley
items.summary:
CEO was viewed as ‘irreplaceable’, but recklessness of affair with a woman regarded by US officials as a Chinese spy made him a political liability

Half the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe.

It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability.

Continue reading...

items.title: AI helped UK defy expectations – but will economy’s resilience fizzle out?
items.summary:
Despite John Healey’s defiance, the economy faces threats from a tech slowdown and energy bills this winter

  • AI helps UK economy grow at fastest pace for more than two years

The forecasters were clear when John Healey became chancellor in July: Britain’s resilience to the war in the Middle East would not last. The global economic headwinds were too strong, inflation was beginning to rise and growth would slow to a trickle.

Four months into the job, the economy is continuing to defy expectations after growing by 0.7% in the third quarter – the fastest expansion in two and a half years. It puts the UK on course to be the second-fastest growing G7 economy this year.

items.title: Bots in the boardroom: Could an AI ever replace board directors?
items.summary:
Board members are busy putting AI to work, using it to summarize lengthy papers, track market trends, and answer their questions. But some boards are going one step further and deploying AI in the boardroom. 

Diligent makes software that directors use to share documents and run meetings. When its boss, Brian Strafford, told one chief executive about the company’s new board bot, their response hinted at where the technology may be headed. “I love the idea,” he said. “I’d immediately replace a couple of my board members with AI.” He then asked whether it could be priced at half what he pays his directors. “I want to make them nervous,” the CEO said.

The exchange, though spoken half in jest, raises a serious question: How far can, and should, AI go in the boardroom? While many executives remain hesitant about using AI in this setting, others are experimenting with creating digital replicas of colleagues to rehearse potentially difficult boardroom discussions, according to Stafford.

In April, Lloyds Banking Group became the first FTSE 100 firm to acknowledge it deploys an AI agent to support boardroom activities, The Times reported. Its executives and directors reportedly use the bot for agenda planning and analysis before high-level meetings, and to help mitigate human bias.

Pippa Begg, chief executive of Board Intelligence, which builds AI software for boards, says that AI could eventually sit in on meetings and be “able to almost interrupt and say: ‘Hang on, I think you’re falling into this trap.’ Or: ‘I disagree.’” However, giving it a formal legal vote, she added,…
items.t: Bots in the boardroom: Could an AI ever replace board directors?
